name: DACI Decision-Making Framework
use_case: A role-assignment framework for cross-functional decisions, naming exactly one Driver, one Approver, multiple Contributors, and the Informed for a specific decision. Best used when decisions are stalling because nobody knows who actually owns the call versus who is consulted versus who is just kept in the loop.
strengths: forces a single Approver — eliminates decision-by-committee drift
trivial to facilitate — one table, one meeting
scales from team-level to org-level decisions
creates an audit trail for retrospectives
weaknesses: doesn't help if the disagreement is *substantive* (use a different method first)
tempting to overuse — not every decision needs a DACI
the Approver role can feel autocratic in flat cultures
requires the Driver to be senior enough to push back on the Approver
use_cases: Three department heads each assume one of the others has signed off on changing the customer refund policy, so the same question has been reopened in three leadership meetings running.
After a reorganisation merged two departments, both former heads believe they have the final say on which reporting standard the combined team adopts, and staff do not know whose instruction counts.
A programme lead starting a multi-team initiative wants each major call recorded with who proposed it, who signed it off and who only needed the outcome, so later disputes can be traced.
A pricing change has twenty people copied on every thread and each expects to weigh in; the owner needs to separate the few whose expertise is needed from the many who just need to hear the result.
The manager who is supposed to approve a high-stakes cross-team decision keeps collecting opinions instead of making the call.
A team lead preparing a decision document for a cross-departmental change wants the approver, the advisers and those to be informed named before options are discussed.
